content.title: A Super El Niño Is Possible Later This Year. Here's What That Could Mean For Hurricane Season And Winter
content.text: The Latest Update About The Upcoming El NiñoA super El Niño is increasingly possible later this year, and that could have significant global impacts on rainfall and temperatures from summer through winter, as well as the 2026 hurricane season.The Latest ForecastThe central and eastern equatorial Pacific waters have transitioned away from a persistent La Niña over the past month.You can see this in the animation from NOAA's Climate Prediction Center below. Note the warmer than average ocean water encroaching from the west near the equator while the cool anomalies are fading.Weather in your inboxBy signing up you agree to the Terms & Privacy Policy. Unsubscribe at any time.This animation shows ocean surface temperature anomalies in degrees Celsius over the tropical Pacific Ocean from Jan. 14 - April 1, 2026. (NOAA/CPC)An El Niño is expected to develop quickly by this summer and last into the fall and winter, according to the latest computer model forecasts. NOAA calculated a 61% of that happening sometime from May through July, according to their monthly update released Thursday.(MORE: Here's Your Complete Guide To El Niño?)El Niño is a periodic warming of water in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that can affect global weather patterns for months. There have been 27 El Niños since 1950, with one happening on average every 3 to 4 years.You can see this tongue of anomalously warm water forecast by one of the computer models in the map below, stretching from the coast of South America to the central Pacific Ocean near the equator.The forecast sea-surface temperature anomalies — in degrees Celsius — from August-October 2026. The potential super El Niño is depicted by the darkest brown contours from South America to the central equatorial Pacific Ocean. (European Centre For Medium-Range Weather Forecasts)'Super El Niño' - What Is It?This won't be your garden-variety, weak El Niño.NOAA's monthly update assigned a roughly 50% chance this El Niño would become strong, in which ocean surface temperatures are at least 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than average.(WATCH: What Is A Super El Niño?)By fall or early winter, NOAA assigned a 1 in 4 chance it could intensify into a super El Niño, in which those warm ocean anomalies reach at least 2 degrees Celsius.These are the percent chances of weak, moderate, strong and super El Niño by three-month period through January 2027, as issued in NOAA's April 9, 2026, update. (NOAA/CPC)Computer models are also trending toward a super El Niño, as you can see below.The latest El Niño ensemble model forecasts as of the time of publish from the ECMWF (left) and from the NMME (right). Temperature anomalies are in degrees Celsius.(Left: ECMWF; Right: NOAA/CPC)These intense El Niños are more rare.There have been only five since 1950, the last occurring 11 years ago from 2015-16. They also occured in 1997-98, 1991-92, 1982-83 and 1972-73. Super El Niños have also been documented in 1888-89 and 1877-78.Why It Could Be 'Super'The trend in the various computer models shown above and the extremity of their forecast is one thing.However, model forecasts of El Niño and La Niña have historically struggled in the spring. It's what scientists call the "spring predictability barrier".Usually in spring, we're transitioning out of La Niña or El Niño, and each of those typically reaches their peak in late fall or early winter, many months down the road. Any weather forecast has more uncertainty the farther out in time you look. And forecasting a transition from one phase to another is also more difficult. Think of how hard it is for an economist to forecast a change, say from a recession to a bull market.But another reason boosting confidence in an eventual super El Niño is a surge of westerly winds near the equator in the western Pacific called a westerly wind burst."These periods of strong winds blowing west to east are pushing warm waters onto the equator and driving them eastward, contributing to rapid warming in the eastern Pacific," wrote Paul Roundy, a University of Albany professor and El Niño expert, in an email to weather.com.Previous studies have shown these bursts happen more frequently and are stronger prior to and during El Niños.Roundy said the strength of the westerly wind burst in early April "is likely to be the strongest in over 50 years, and probably in the last century." In fact, twin tropical cyclones on either side of the equator — Cyclone Maila and a soon-to-form tropical cyclone near Guam — will only give additional juice to the westerly wind burst.This may wash over the typical spring predictability barrier."The likelihood of this event (stronger El Niño) failing, especially given highly confident westerly wind forecasts over the next two weeks, must be small," Roundy added.NOAA's update did pump the brakes a little on the super potential, stressing that it depends on how persistent the anomalous westerly winds are through summer to keep pushing that warmer water eastward into the El Niño zone of the equatorial Pacific.El Niño’s Potential ImpactsFirst, some disclaimers.El Niño (and its opposite, La Niña) is only one influence on the global weather pattern. Also, every El Niño is different, much like every hurricane can have its own idiosyncrasies.But, in general, the stronger the El Niño, the more likely its typical impacts on global weather will happen.Here are some of those potential impacts.Hurricane seasonA stronger El Niño tends to produce more sinking air and stronger wind shear in parts of the Atlantic Basin, both hostile to hurricanes.(MORE: 2026 Hurricane Season Outlook)So, in general, most stronger El Niño Atlantic hurricane seasons are quieter than average. That's not always the case, as the 2023 season illustrated.Meanwhile, eastern and central Pacific hurricane seasons are typically more active during strong El Niños.WinterIn winter, the southern, or subtropical, branch of the jet stream usually is turbocharged in a stronger El Niño.That means a wetter winter usually is the result across the southern tier of states from parts of California and the Desert Southwest to Florida and the Southeast. This could also mean more snow across these areas if the air is cold enough, as we illustrated in a previous deep dive.Meanwhile, much of the northern U.S. typically has a milder and drier winter during a stronger El Niño, from the Northwest and northern Rockies to the Northern Plains and Midwest.Global PrecipitationEl Niño's impacts typically extend around the globe. Those are highlighted on the map below.For example, parts of Africa, India, Australia, the Philippines, Indonesia, the Caribbean and northern South America trend markedly drier during El Niño.On the other hand, warm water and lighter trade winds typically sets the table for heavier rain in parts of Ecuador and Peru. Parts of eastern Africa, central Asia, Chile, Uruguay and Paraguay are also usually wetter than average during El Niño.Typical global precipitation impacts during an El Niño.(NOAA)Global TemperaturesOne impact we're highly confident about is a spike in global temperatures during this El Niño. At the risk of oversimplifying, all this extra equatorial Pacific Ocean heat is released into the atmosphere, and all large swaths of drier conditions allow plentiful sunshine to heat the surface.As the graph below nicely illustrates, the large majority of El Niños have triggered temperature spikes, including the last "non-super" El Niño in 2023.The previous super El Niño crushed previous global temperature records in 2015 and 2016. Those two years remain among the top 10 warmest years for the planet, all of which have occurred since 2015.Given last year was the planet's third warmest year, it seems like a slam dunk that new heat records will be set in 2026, possibly again in 2027.From a climate change angle, this is worrisome.A December 2025 study found super El Niño events can drive sudden "climate regime shifts" in both temperatures and precipitation, and that this effect could be increasing in a warming world.Monthly global temperature anomalies in degrees Celsius from 1950 through February 2026. El Niño months are denoted in red, La Niña months are in blue, and months in a neutral phase are in gray. (NOAA/NCEI)Jonathan Erdman is a senior meteorologist at weather.com and has been covering national and international weather since 1996. Extreme and bizarre weather are his favorite topics.
